title: Problem Set 8
markdown:
## What this covers

This chapter is Problem Set 8 of Berkeley's Stat243, which recurs across three offerings (fall
2021, fall 2024, fall 2025) built around one central question: when part of what determines a
likelihood is unobserved — because a continuous outcome is reported only as its sign (probit
regression) or only as "exceeded a threshold" (censored regression) — how do you fit the model, and
how do you check the fit against a second, independent method? Every offering asks for an EM
algorithm built on the missing piece, and a second, direct maximization of the observed-data
log-likelihood with a general-purpose optimizer, so the two can be checked against each other. It
assumes the course's Unit 11 lecture on the EM algorithm (its $X/Y/Z$ notation for observed,
complete, and latent data, and the E-step/M-step recipe), ordinary linear and logistic regression,
and the standard normal density $\phi$ and CDF $\Phi$. Depending on the offering it also assumes
`scipy.optimize` and JAX or PyTorch automatic differentiation (fall 2024, fall 2025), or R's
`optim()` (fall 2021); fall 2021 additionally draws on Unit 9's importance sampling.

## The machinery every version of the assignment leans on

Two things recur, in slightly different costumes, across every offering.

**A normal variable seen only through a threshold.** In the probit variant (fall 2024) the whole
outcome is latent: $y_i = I(z_i>0)$ where $z_i\sim\mathcal N(X_i^\top\beta,1)$, so knowing $y_i$
says only which side of zero $z_i$ landed on. In the censored-regression variant (fall 2025, fall
2021) only some observations are hidden: $Y_i\sim\mathcal N(\beta_0+\beta_1 x_i,\sigma^2)$ is
reported in full unless it exceeds a fixed threshold $\tau$, in which case only the fact of
exceedance is recorded — the assignment's own real-world examples are pollutant concentrations
reported as "below the limit of detection," and tax records that report incomes above some cutoff
simply as exceeding it. (The fall 2025 source calls the covariate $b_i$ rather than $x_i$; this
chapter uses $x_i$ throughout for both variants.) In both cases, the EM algorithm's E-step needs the
conditional distribution of a normal variable given that it lies above (or below) a cutoff — a
truncated normal — and specifically only its first two moments:
$$
E(W\mid W>\tau) = \mu + \sigma\rho(\tau^*), \qquad
V(W\mid W>\tau) = \sigma^2\bigl(1+\tau^*\rho(\tau^*)-\rho(\tau^*)^2\bigr),
$$
$$
\rho(\tau^*) = \frac{\phi(\tau^*)}{1-\Phi(\tau^*)}, \qquad \tau^* = \frac{\tau-\mu}{\sigma},
$$
attributed in the assignment to Johnson and Kotz's reference volumes on distributions (Wikipedia's
page on the truncated normal distribution gives the same formulae in more general form). These are
exactly the quantities the E-step plugs in for the unobserved $z_i$ or $Y_i$, and they appear,
unchanged, in every EM derivation asked for below.

**Checking EM against a direct numerical maximization.** Every offering also asks for the same
observed-data log-likelihood maximized directly — with `scipy.optimize.minimize` and the BFGS method
(fall 2024, fall 2025) or R's `optim()` (fall 2021) — as an independent check: a correct EM
derivation and a correct direct maximization should land on the same estimates. Three practical
snags recur. First, BFGS can fail to converge from bad starting values, which is worth mapping
directly by trying several starting points and checking, where BFGS fails, whether Nelder-Mead still
finds the optimum. Second, a variance-type parameter such as $\sigma^2$ is naturally constrained to
be positive, which an unconstrained optimizer does not respect, so the R offering asks you to
consider reparameterizing it (and the `parscale` argument, which rescales parameters relative to
one another before the optimizer sees them). Third, the Hessian at the optimum is needed for
standard errors, and the object `scipy`'s `minimize` hands back as `hess_inv` is not that — it is
only the approximation BFGS built up along the way, not a numerical derivative evaluated at the
optimum itself — so the Python offerings ask for the real thing computed separately: with
`numdifftools`, and again with a JAX or PyTorch Hessian built by automatic differentiation, using
just-in-time compilation (`jit`/`@jit` in JAX, `torch.compile` in PyTorch) so the objective, its
gradient, and its Hessian are all fast enough to compare on timing as well as on the answer.

## Exercises

### 1. EM for a normal seen only through a threshold

Two variants of the same problem were assigned; work whichever matches your course offering.

**Probit-regression variant (fall 2024).** The probit model for a binary outcome,
$Y_i\sim\text{Ber}(p_i)$ with $p_i=P(Y_i=1)=\Phi(X_i^\top\beta)$, can be rewritten with one latent
variable per observation, $y_i=I(z_i>0)$ with $z_i\sim\mathcal N(X_i^\top\beta,1)$.

a. Design an EM algorithm to estimate $\beta$, taking the complete data to be $\{Y,Z\}$. Use the
   truncated-normal moments above; keep $\beta$ distinct from its current value $\beta^t$
   throughout, both in the expectation and in the maximization; and make sure your calculation uses
   the fact that, for each $i$, you already know whether $z_i$ is bigger or smaller than $0$ from
   $y_i$. The expected log-likelihood should be maximizable analytically, and is worth recognizing
   as an ordinary regression of some new quantities $m_i$ — functions of $\beta^t$ and $y_i$ — on
   $X$.
b. Propose a way to get reasonable starting values for $\beta$.
c. Write a Python function implementing the algorithm, using the starting values from (b); existing
   regression functions may be used for the update step. Include a stopping criterion.
d. Test the function on data simulated from the model with $n=100$, choosing $\beta_1$ (by trial and
   error — e.g. simulating for a candidate $\beta_1$ and fitting an ordinary logistic regression to
   check the signal-to-noise ratio, then adjusting) so that $\hat\beta_1/\text{se}(\hat\beta_1)
   \approx 2$, with $\beta_2=\beta_3=0$.

**Censored-regression variant (fall 2025, fall 2021).** With $Y_i\sim\mathcal
N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)$ and $n_c$ of the $n$ observations censored (reported only as
exceeding $\tau$):

a. Design an EM algorithm for $\theta=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2)$, taking the complete data to be
   the observed values together with the actual (unobserved) values behind the censored ones. Using
   the EM notation from the lecture, treat the fact that a censored $Y_i$ exceeds $\tau$ as part of
   $X$, alongside the fully observed values; write the complete-data log-likelihood as a sum of a
   term for the observed values and a term for the censored ones, conditioning the latter on
   exceeding $\tau$; and use the truncated-normal moments above. Keep $\theta$ and $\theta^t$
   distinct throughout. You should find the expected log-likelihood is an ordinary regression of
   $\{Y_{\text{obs}}, m^t\}$ on $\{x\}$, where the $m_i^t$ (functions of $\theta^t$) stand in for the
   censored values; the resulting estimator for $\sigma^2$ should have a numerator equal to the
   usual sum of squares for the observed data plus an extra term, worth interpreting statistically.
   The maximization should again be analytic.
b. Propose starting values for the three parameters as functions of the data.
c. Implement the algorithm — in Python, using `statsmodels` for the regression update (fall 2025);
   or in R, using `lm()` (fall 2021) — with a stopping criterion, and test it on data simulated from
   the course's `ps8.py`/`ps8.R` code at both a modest censoring rate (about 20%) and a high one
   (about 80%).

### 2. Checking EM against a direct maximum-likelihood fit

The observed-data log-likelihood can also be maximized directly. For the censored-regression model
this replaces the truncated-normal term used in the EM derivation with the tail probability
$P(Y_i>\tau)$ for each censored point.

**Python/JAX or PyTorch variant (fall 2024, fall 2025).**

a. Write the negative log-likelihood as an objective function in JAX or PyTorch syntax.
b. Fit it with `scipy.optimize.minimize` (BFGS), and compare the iteration count against your EM
   implementation — the two should agree on the estimates, which is itself a check on your EM
   derivation and code. Fall 2024 also asks for standard errors from the Hessian at this point,
   computed with `numdifftools` rather than trusted from `hess_inv` (per the note above), watching
   for loss-of-precision warnings that may mean switching JAX or PyTorch to 64-bit floats. Fall 2025
   instead asks you to consider reparameterizing before fitting, deferring the Hessian comparison to
   (d).
c. Search for starting values that make BFGS fail to converge. Do the same starting values converge
   under Nelder-Mead?
d. Build a gradient function by automatic differentiation, JIT-compile the objective and gradient,
   and refit with BFGS using the supplied gradient; confirm you recover the same estimates as in
   (b), and compare iteration count and timing against relying on scipy's numerical differentiation.
   Then build a Hessian function the same way and use it to get standard errors at the optimum.
   Fall 2024 compares this Hessian to the `numdifftools`-based one from (b); fall 2025 compares it
   instead to the `hess_inv` returned by `minimize`, with the same caution that `hess_inv` is only
   an approximation built up during the BFGS iterations, not a numerical derivative at the optimum.

**R/`optim()` variant (fall 2021).** Using `optim()` with the BFGS method — considering
reparameterization, and possibly the `parscale` argument — estimate the parameters and standard
errors for your simulated test cases, and compare the iteration counts of EM and BFGS; together they
are a check on each other.

### 3. Importance sampling and tail weight (fall 2021)

Consider estimating $\phi=E(X)$ and $\phi=E(X^2)$ under a density $f$ by importance sampling from a
different density $g$, using the Pareto density $p(x)=\beta\alpha^\beta/x^{\beta+1}$ for
$\alpha<x<\infty$, $\alpha,\beta>0$ (mean $\beta\alpha/(\beta-1)$ for $\beta>1$, variance
$\beta\alpha^2/[(\beta-1)^2(\beta-2)]$ for $\beta>2$, neither existing otherwise).

a. Does the Pareto's tail decay faster or slower than an exponential's?
b. Let $f$ be an exponential density with rate $1$, shifted right by $2$ (so $f(x)=0$ for $x<2$),
   and pretend you cannot sample from it directly. Using importance sampling with $g$ a Pareto
   distribution ($\alpha=2$, $\beta=3$) and $m=10{,}000$ draws, estimate $E(X)$ and $E(X^2)$ and
   compare to the known values for the shifted exponential. Since $\text{Var}(\hat\phi)\propto
   \text{Var}\bigl(h(X)f(X)/g(X)\bigr)$, plot histograms of both $h(x)f(x)/g(x)$ and the raw weights
   $f(x)/g(x)$, and note whether any extreme weights would dominate $\hat\phi$.
c. Now swap roles: let $f$ be the Pareto above (pretending you cannot sample from it) and $g$ the
   shifted exponential, and answer the same questions, comparing to the known Pareto moments.

### 4. Mapping a genuinely multimodal objective (fall 2021)

Using the "helical valley" function (`ps8.R` in the course repository), plot slices of it — holding
one input fixed and plotting the function as a 2-d surface in the other two, e.g. with `image()`,
`contour()`, `persp()`, or their `ggplot2` equivalents — to see how it behaves. Then use `optim()`
and `nlm()` (or `optimx()`) to find its minimum from a range of starting points, and use what you
find to assess whether it has more than one local minimum.

### 5. (Extra credit) A small neural network for nonlinear regression (fall 2025)

Fit a basic one- or two-layer neural network (most easily built in PyTorch) to a nonlinear
regression/prediction problem with a single predictor. Explore how sensitive the fit is to starting
values, choice of optimizer, and learning rate, and look for signs of overfitting — bearing in mind
that deep networks are often surprisingly robust to it despite having many parameters.
